fields.title: Mary Slessor (For Teens)
fields.description: From the age of eleven, Mary Slessor worked at a loom in a Dundee factory, and on Saturday nights she sat up with her mother waiting for her father to come home drunk. At twenty-seven she sailed for Calabar, learned Efik so well that people said she spoke it better than they did, and walked alone into Okoyong, where she sat beside chained prisoners facing the poison ordeal and took in the twin babies others had been taught to throw away. This teen edition tells her story straight: the fear, the babies she buried, the friend who never believed, the power she borrowed, and the love nobody doubted.

qa.question: Who was Mary Slessor?
qa.answer: A Scottish factory girl, born in Aberdeen in 1848 and raised in Dundee, who went to Calabar, in what is now south-eastern Nigeria, in 1876 as a teacher for the United Presbyterian Church of Scotland. She spent almost forty years among the Efik, Okoyong and Ibibio peoples, protecting twins and their mothers and people accused of witchcraft, sitting as a magistrate, and opening the Enyong Creek to the gospel. She died at Use in 1915.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It names her father's drinking, the killing of twins, the poison ordeal and the killings at chiefs' funerals, the many babies she buried, her loneliness and dark moods, and her use of laudanum. It also names her faults: she could be harsh, she struck people in her court, and she leaned on British colonial power and sometimes spoke of it as Christian.

qa.question: What did she mean by “the woman's God”?
qa.answer: A chief told her that a woman going into a war only proved her ignorance. She replied, “In measuring the woman's power, you have evidently forgotten to take into account the woman's God.” She meant that what she could do never depended on her own strength, which she knew was small, but on God.

qa.question: Did Mary Slessor end the killing of twins in Nigeria?
qa.answer: No, and she would not have claimed it. The Efik rulers of Calabar, with the British consul, banned it in 1849 and 1851, missionaries rescued twins from 1852, and the practice went on in some places after her death. What she did was carry protection for twins and their mothers into districts the old agreements did not reach. In 1898 she said she had saved fifty-one twins.

qa.question: How did she treat the people she lived among?
qa.answer: She learned Efik so well that people said she spoke it better than many Efik did, ate local food, and lived among the people rather than apart. She said, “After all we are foreigners, and they own the country.” She could also be imperious and shared some prejudices of her time. Her closest friend, Ma Eme, never became a Christian, and Mary honoured her all her life.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Mary Slessor, which draws mainly on her own letters as printed by her first biographer, W. P. Livingstone, and checks them against Scottish records, Mary Kingsley's eyewitness account and modern historians in Scotland and Nigeria. A few stories, like the gang leader with the lead weight, rest on her own later telling, and this edition says so.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from her story?
qa.answer: That courage is not the absence of fear; that God can use a shy, poorly schooled young person from a hard home; that you can stand with people everyone else rejects; and that strength is often given only once you begin.

qa.question: Why did she never marry?
qa.answer: She was engaged to Charles Morrison, a young teacher at the mission. She would not leave Okoyong, the Church would not send him there, and then his health failed. She wrote that her life “was laid on His altar for that people long ago, and I would not take one jot or tittle of it back.”

fields.title: Saturday Nights
fields.body_html:
“Like as a father pitieth his children, So Jehovah pitieth them that fear him.” — Psalm 103:13 (ASV)

Mary Mitchell Slessor was born on 2 December 1848 in Gilcomston, on the edge of Aberdeen in Scotland. Her mother, also called Mary, was a gentle woman with a deep, quiet faith. Her Church had just started a mission far away, at a place in West Africa called Calabar, and she followed every report from it. The reports were read aloud at home and talked over. “I had my missionary enthusiasm for Calabar in particular from her,” Mary said long afterwards.

Her father, Robert, was a shoemaker who moved from job to job. And Robert Slessor drank. He lost his work, and in 1859 the family moved south to the factory city of Dundee, hoping he could make a fresh start where nobody knew him. The furniture was sold to pay for the move. It didn't help. Every penny he could lay his hands on went on drink.

So Mary's mother, who was not strong, went out to work in a factory. Mary, still a child, was sent with parcels to the pawnbroker. She ran there by the quietest back streets, so that her friends from church would not see her. Every Saturday night, after the younger children were in bed, mother and daughter sat sewing in silence, waiting for the sound of unsteady footsteps on the stair, and now and then praying to calm their hearts. When he came in, he would sometimes throw into the fire the supper they had gone without so that he could eat. Sometimes Mary was put out into the street, and wandered alone in the dark, crying.

The family hid all this. On Sunday, few families looked brighter in church. Mary rarely spoke of her father for the rest of her life. The memory made her shy and afraid of speaking in public. It also, her first biographer thought, made her a fierce defender of children and of anyone weak.

Yet Mary was not a gloomy child. She remembered herself as “a wild lassie.” Her faith began when an old widow in the tenements brought some girls in from the cold, pointed at her fire, and warned them that a worse fire waited for souls who would not turn to Christ. The picture kept Mary awake at night, and she “repented and believed.” Fear brought her to the door. But inside she found a kingdom of love, and she never tried to frighten anyone else into it.

Her father died in 1870, when she was twenty-one. Years later she wrote something she rarely said about her own life:

“I know what it is to pray long years and never get the answer. I had to pray for my father. But I know my heavenly Father so well that I can leave it with Him for the lower fatherhood.”

That is the honest heart of this chapter. She prayed for years, and her father did not change. She did not pretend he had. But she found another Father, the one in the psalm at the top of this page, who pities weakness instead of despising it.

Maybe your home has a secret your family works hard to hide: drinking, anger, money that never lasts the week. If so, hear this plainly. It is not your fault, and you are not the only one. Keeping it secret is not your job. If you are not safe at home, tell a safe adult: a teacher, a pastor, a relative, a doctor, or a helpline where you live. Mary's mother prayed, and she also kept her children going. Both matter.

One thing to do this week: write down one prayer you have prayed for a long time without seeing an answer. Under it, write Mary's words: “I can leave it with Him.” Then tell God honestly how that feels. If something at home is not safe, talk to one trusted adult this week.

study_questions.question: What was Mary's home like in Dundee?
study_questions.answer: Her father drank away the family's money. Her mother worked in a factory, Mary ran to the pawnbroker, and on Saturday nights they waited in fear for him to come home.

study_questions.question: Was her prayer for her father answered?
study_questions.answer: No. He never changed, and she said so honestly. She learned to trust her heavenly Father with what she could not understand.

study_questions.question: How did Mary's own conversion shape the way she spoke to others about God?
study_questions.answer: She was first frightened into faith, but found a kingdom of love, so she never tried to scare anyone into it. She drew people by kindness instead.

fields.title: A Changed Lassie
fields.body_html:
“It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.” — Lamentations 3:27 (ASV)

At eleven, Mary went to work at Baxter Brothers, one of the biggest textile firms in Dundee. She was a “half-timer”: half the day in the factory, half in the factory school. Soon she was full-time, and went to school at night. The day ran from six in the morning to six at night. She got up at five to do housework before she left, and there was more waiting when she got home. In the weaving-shed the belts whirred overhead and the shuttles flew, and the noise was so loud that talking was almost impossible.

She became a skilled weaver, eventually running two wide looms at once, and she stayed at the loom for about fourteen years. When she brought home her first wages, her mother wept over them and said they were too sacred to spend. They didn't stay unspent for long. The family needed every shilling. Her younger brother Robert died of croup in 1860. Her brother William died of tuberculosis in 1870, not yet twenty, and five months later her father died. At twenty-one, Mary was the head of the household in all but name.

She had almost no schooling, but she was hungry to learn. She propped a book open on the loom and read when the work allowed, and read walking to work through the grey streets. Above all she read the Bible. Once a girl asked her for something to read, and Mary handed over her own Bible: “Take that; it has made me a changed lassie.”

Outside the factory, her life was the church. Wishart Church stood in the middle of a slum, and gangs of boys ran the streets with nobody to control them. When the church opened a mission for them, Mary volunteered to teach. The older boys came to wreck the meetings, and they threw mud at her when she preached outdoors.

One story from those years has no named witness; as far as we know, it rests on her own later telling, so take it as a remembered story. A gang surrounded her one night. Their leader swung a lead weight on a cord round her head, closer and closer, until it grazed her forehead. She didn't move. At last he dropped it. “She's game, boys,” he said, and the whole gang followed her into the meeting.

Here's the surprising thing: Mary Slessor was afraid of crowds, afraid of speaking in public, and afraid of cows in fields, all her life. Her courage was not the absence of fear. It was staying put when she wanted to run.

She was also honest about her limits. A famous book told her to practise meditation, and it made her miserable. “I canna meditate,” she told a friend, “and Doddridge says it is necessary for the soul. If I try to meditate my mind just goes a' roads.” Her friend told her to stop worrying and go and work, “for that's what God means us to do.” She did. Her prayers were always the prayers of a busy woman, said in the middle of the work.

Lamentations was written in the ruins of Jerusalem, and it doesn't pretend the yoke is light. It says carrying it young can be good, because of what it teaches. The loom made Mary tough and patient, and it gave her a working woman's respect for the poor. Years later, standing among African women carrying loads on their heads, she never looked down on them. She had been a labourer herself.

Maybe you are carrying more than other people your age: work, younger siblings, a parent who leans on you. God doesn't waste those years. They can grow something in you that easier years can't.

One thing to do this week: pick one dull or heavy job you have to do this week, at home, school or work. Before you start, give it to God in one sentence: “This is for you.” Notice whether it changes how you do it.

fields.title: Scores of Casks
fields.body_html:
“And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, Here am I; send me.” — Isaiah 6:8 (ASV)

The mission Mary's mother followed so closely did not begin in Scotland. It began in Jamaica, among people who had been enslaved. Many Africans taken to the Caribbean had been shipped from the Bight of Biafra, and many had passed through Calabar. When slavery ended in the British colonies in the 1830s, freed Jamaicans who had become Christians began asking whether the gospel that reached them in captivity could go back to the land their parents came from. In 1843 the king and chiefs of the Efik towns of Calabar sent an invitation, offering land and a welcome. In 1846 a minister named Hope Waddell led a small party there, including Jamaicans of African descent.

So the Calabar mission was first imagined by freed Africans, invited by African rulers, and carried out with the help of both.

Mary's mother longed for her son John to be a missionary. But John's health failed. He emigrated to New Zealand for a warmer climate and died soon after landing. Mary grieved, and a quiet question formed: could she take her brother's place? She told no one for a long time.

She knew what people said about West Africa. It was called the white man's grave. Fever killed Europeans so fast that the mission graveyards were full of young men and women who hadn't lasted a year. A fellow student remembered her answer: Calabar was the post of danger, and therefore the post of honour. Few would volunteer, so she would.

In 1874 news came that the explorer David Livingstone had died in Africa, and Scotland was stirred. Mary decided it was time. Her sisters were now working, and she planned to send money home from Africa so her mother would not suffer. In May 1875 she offered herself to her Church's Foreign Mission Board and was accepted as a teacher for Calabar. She was twenty-six, a factory worker with little education, terrified of public speaking.

The night before she left Dundee for training in Edinburgh, in March 1876, a friend found her crying at the entrance of the close where she lived. “Good-bye,” she said. And then, with passion: “Pray for me!”

In Edinburgh she gave her first talk, to a meeting of women. She took Pilate's question about Jesus, “What then shall I do unto Jesus who is called Christ?” Christ was standing before them just as he stood before Pilate, she told them. “Dear women,” she said, “you must do something with Him: you must reject Him or you must accept Him. What are you going to do?” No threats about hell-fire. Just the question, left with them.

She sailed from Liverpool on 5 August 1876, on a steamer called the Ethiopia. Two friends from Dundee watched the cargo being loaded. Much of it was casks of spirits for the West African trade. “Scores of casks!” she said. “And only one missionary!” It was a joke, and it was also a judgement. The daughter of Robert Slessor knew exactly what drink did to a home. She was about to see what it did to whole communities.

Look at the order in Isaiah's call. He didn't volunteer because he felt brave. He first saw how holy God was and cried, “Woe is me!” Only after he had been forgiven did he hear the question and say, “Here am I; send me.” Mary wasn't a heroine when she said yes. She was a frightened young woman who knew how much God had done for her.

You don't need to feel ready, gifted or fearless to be useful to God. You need to have been loved by him, and to know it.

One thing to do this week: ask God Isaiah's question in your own words: “Is there somewhere you want to send me, even somewhere small?” Then do the first small thing that comes to mind, like a message to someone who is lonely or an offer of help.

study_questions.answer: Freed African Jamaicans who had become Christians first imagined it, and the king and chiefs of the Efik towns of Calabar invited the missionaries in 1843.

study_questions.question: What did Mary mean by “Scores of casks! And only one missionary!”?
study_questions.answer: The same ship carrying her to Africa was carrying huge amounts of alcohol. She had seen what drink did to her own family, and it was a sad joke about which cargo Europe was sending more of.

study_questions.question: Why does the order of Isaiah's call matter?
study_questions.answer: Isaiah first saw God's holiness and was forgiven, and only then said, “Here am I; send me.” The call starts with God's mercy, not with a person's bravery or gifts.

fields.title: Not in Haste
fields.body_html:
“he that believeth shall not be in haste.” — Isaiah 28:16 (ASV)

In September 1876 the Ethiopia steamed up the wide, muddy estuary of the Cross and Calabar rivers, past mangrove swamps and the ruins of the pens where enslaved people had once waited for the ships, and anchored off Duke Town.

Calabar was not part of any European empire. The towns along the river were ruled by the Efik, who had grown rich for two centuries as traders with Europe, first in slaves and later in palm oil. Mary quickly learned that this was an ordered society, with laws and customs as strong as any in Europe. People lived in great Houses under a chief. A powerful men's society, Ekpe (Europeans called it Egbo), made and enforced the law. The people believed in a high God, but lived in fear of spirits and witchcraft. A death was rarely thought natural: someone was to blame, and the accused could be made to drink poison made from the Calabar bean to prove their innocence. When a great man died, slaves and wives might be killed to go with him.

At Creek Town she met King Eyo Honesty VII, a Christian king who led worship in his own town. He was so pleased to hear that her mother followed the mission that he wrote to Mrs. Slessor, and the two wrote back and forth: an African king and a poor widow in a Scottish tenement.

Mary was determined to learn Efik properly. She learned it from the people, by ear, and in time visitors said she spoke Efik better than many Efik did.

She also met an uncomfortable truth. In a poor part of Duke Town she spoke against the rum some men were selling, and one answered in the coast's pidgin: “What for white man bring them rum suppose them rum no be good? He be god-man bring the rum, then what for god-man talk so?” Her biographer wrote simply: “She cannot answer the man.” The drink came from countries that called themselves Christian. She never forgot it.

Fever hit her again and again. “I want my home and my mother,” she wrote. After a furlough home she came back in 1880 to run the station at Old Town. There she began living on local food, and her colleagues thought she simply liked living like the people. The truth was that she was sending most of her salary home to her mother and sisters, and was, as her biographer put it, “too loyal to her home and too proud of spirit to reveal the reason.”

At Old Town she met the custom that would become the cause of her life. The birth of twins was seen as a disaster: one child, people believed, had an evil spirit for a father. Twin babies were killed and left in the bush, and their mother was driven out to live alone. Mary was not the first to fight this. The Efik rulers, with the British consul, had banned it as early as 1849 and 1851, and missionaries had been rescuing twins since 1852. But a law doesn't change a belief, and the killing went on in secret.

She rescued a pair of twins. While she was out, relatives took the boy by a trick and killed him. In 1883, so ill she had to be carried onto the ship, she took the girl home to Scotland. Her name was Atim Eso. She would be baptised Janie.

Mary was impatient by nature, and she wrote the verse at the top of this chapter as a reminder to herself: the one who trusts God does not need to rush. She would see very little harvest in her lifetime.

You probably want results fast, from friends, from school, from God. Some of the best things grow slowly.

One thing to do this week: choose one thing you have been impatient about, a friendship, a skill, a prayer. Instead of forcing it this week, do one faithful step and leave the rest with God.

study_questions.question: Who ruled Calabar when Mary arrived?
study_questions.answer: The Efik, through their own Houses and the Ekpe society. No European power governed it in 1876.

study_questions.question: What could Mary not answer when she spoke against the rum?
study_questions.answer: A man asked why, if rum was bad, the “god-man” from Christian countries brought it. The trade came from Europe, and she had no answer.

study_questions.question: Was Mary the first person to oppose the killing of twins?
study_questions.answer: No. The Efik rulers and the British consul had banned it in 1849 and 1851, and missionaries had rescued twins since 1852. Mary carried the fight into places the law did not reach.

fields.body_text: “he that believeth shall not be in haste.” — Isaiah 28:16 (ASV) In September 1876 the Ethiopia steamed up the wide, muddy estuary of the Cross and Calabar rivers, past mangrove swamps and the ruins of the pens where enslaved people had once waited for the ships, and anchored off Duke Town. Calabar was not part of any European empire. The towns along the river were ruled by the Efik, who had grown rich for two centuries as traders with Europe, first in slaves and later in palm oil. Mary quickly learned that this was an ordered society, with laws and customs as strong as any in Europe. People lived in great Houses under a chief. A powerful men's society, Ekpe (Europeans called it Egbo), made and enforced the law. The people believed in a high God, but lived in fear of spirits and witchcraft. A death was rarely thought natural: someone was to blame, and the accused could be made to drink poison made from the Calabar bean to prove their innocence. When a great man died, slaves and wives might be killed to go with him. At Creek Town she met King Eyo Honesty VII, a Christian king who led worship in his own town. He was so pleased to hear that her mother followed the mission that he wrote to Mrs. Slessor, and the two wrote back and forth: an African king and a poor widow in a Scottish tenement. Mary was determined to learn Efik properly. She learned it from the people, by ear, and in time visitors said she spoke Efik better than many Efik did. She also met an uncomfortable truth. In a poor part of Duke Town she spoke against the rum some men were selling, and one answered in the coast's pidgin: “What for white man bring them rum suppose them rum no be good? He be god-man bring the rum, then what for god-man talk so?” Her biographer wrote simply: “She cannot answer the man.” The drink came from countries that called themselves Christian. She never forgot it. Fever hit her again and again. “I want my home and my mother,” she wrote. After a furlough home she came back in 1880 to run the station at Old Town. There she began living on local food, and her colleagues thought she simply liked living like the people. The truth was that she was sending most of her salary home to her mother and sisters, and was, as her biographer put it, “too loyal to her home and too proud of spirit to reveal the reason.” At Old Town she met the custom that would become the cause of her life. The birth of twins was seen as a disaster: one child, people believed, had an evil spirit for a father. Twin babies were killed and left in the bush, and their mother was driven out to live alone. Mary was not the first to fight this. The Efik rulers, with the British consul, had banned it as early as 1849 and 1851, and missionaries had been rescuing twins since 1852. But a law doesn't change a belief, and the killing went on in secret. She rescued a pair of twins. While she was out, relatives took the boy by a trick and killed him. In 1883, so ill she had to be carried onto the ship, she took the girl home to Scotland. Her name was Atim Eso. She would be baptised Janie. Mary was impatient by nature, and she wrote the verse at the top of this chapter as a reminder to herself: the one who trusts God does not need to rush. She would see very little harvest in her lifetime. You probably want results fast, from friends, from school, from God. Some of the best things grow slowly. One thing to do this week: choose one thing you have been impatient about, a friendship, a skill, a prayer. Instead of forcing it this week, do one faithful step and leave the rest with God.

fields.title: Stranded and Alone
fields.body_html:
“My flesh and my heart faileth; But God is the strength of my heart and my portion for ever.” — Psalm 73:26 (ASV)

Back in Scotland, Mary spent most of her time at home with her mother and sisters, nursing baby Janie. In Calabar the child was believed to be cursed. In Dundee she was alive and loved. Her twin brother was not.

Asked to speak at meetings, she was so shy that she often could not open her mouth if men were present. But she knew what she believed about reaching people. “Nothing, I believe, will ever touch or raise fallen ones except sympathy,” she wrote to a friend. “They shrink from self-righteousness which would stoop to them, and they hate patronage and pity.” Sympathy and patience were what people needed.

Then her youngest sister, Janie, became seriously ill. Doctors said only a milder climate might save her. Mary asked the mission to let her take her sister to Calabar and live in a mud house together. They refused, kindly. So for a while Mary cut herself loose from the mission and moved her sister and mother to Topsham, a small town in Devon in the south of England. In April 1885 her other sister, Susan, died suddenly in Edinburgh. Mary was now earning nothing, and providing alone for her mother, an invalid sister and an African child.

Before going back to work, she asked her mother something. If the chance ever came to go up-country, into places no missionary had reached, would she let her go? Her mother's answer stayed with Mary all her life:

“You are my child, given to me by God, and I have given you back to Him. When He needs you and where He sends you, there I would have you be.”

She sailed again in November 1885. On New Year's Day 1886 she wrote a long, happy letter home. She ended, “Tell me all your troubles, and be sure you take care of yourselves.”

She never got an answer. Her mother had died in December, within weeks of Mary sailing. Three months later, on 5 March 1886, her sister Janie died too. “I, who all my life have been caring and planning and living for them,” Mary wrote, “am left, as it were, stranded and alone.” On the night the news came, she led her usual prayer meeting and told nobody. Then she wrote:

“Heaven is now nearer to me than Britain, and no one will be anxious about me if I go up-country.”

That is grief talking, and something more. Everything she had worked for since she was eleven had been for her family. Now there was no one left to send money to and no one to worry about her. She was free, with the terrible freedom of the bereaved.

She went to Creek Town, and her house filled up again: little Janie, rescued twins, boys and girls from different families. A baby was brought whose mother had died, and Mary asked the child's owner to lend a woman to nurse it. The answer came back: “Let it die.” Her biographer's comment is four words long: “She let it live.”

In October 1886 the mission decided to send her where she had been asking to go: Okoyong, inland, where no missionary had lived. She borrowed David Livingstone's words: “I am ready to go anywhere, provided it be forward.”

The psalmist says, “My flesh and my heart faileth.” He doesn't pretend to be fine. But he finds that God is still there when everything else is gone. If you are grieving, you don't have to rush to the “but God” part. And if grief ever turns into feeling that you can't go on, tell a safe person: a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

One thing to do this week: think of someone who has lost a person they love, even if it was a while ago. Send them a short message this week saying you remember. Grieving people often feel that everyone else has moved on.

study_questions.question: What did Mary's mother say when Mary asked to go up-country?
study_questions.answer: “You are my child, given to me by God, and I have given you back to Him. When He needs you and where He sends you, there I would have you be.”

study_questions.question: What happened to Mary's family in 1885 and 1886?
study_questions.answer: Her sister Susan died in April 1885, her mother died in December 1885 just after Mary sailed, and her sister Janie died in March 1886.

study_questions.answer: With her family gone, her strongest ties were now in heaven, and there was no one at home to worry if she went into dangerous places.

fields.title: “Father!”
fields.body_html:
“Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for Jehovah thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.” — Joshua 1:9 (ASV)

Okoyong was forest country between the Cross River and the Calabar River, a day's journey inland. Its people were farmers and hunters living in scattered clearings under their own chiefs, and for generations they had been in a long feud with the Efik of Calabar.

The customs that troubled Mary were real, and she described them herself. When a free person fell ill or died, a witch-doctor named those to blame, and they were chained and made to take the poison-bean ordeal, or have boiling oil poured on their hands. When a chief died, slaves and wives were killed to go with him. After careful questioning she later estimated that at least a hundred and fifty lives a year were taken at funerals near her, and as many again by the ordeal. Nobody can check her figures, but they explain why she went. And there was gin everywhere: work, fines and debts were paid in it, and babies were given it.

It took a year of visits before she could go. “I had often a lump in my throat,” she wrote, “and my courage repeatedly threatened to take wings and fly away, though nobody guessed it!” In June 1888 she reached a village called Ekenge. The chief, Edem, welcomed her, and people called her “Mother.” Friends in Creek Town told her nothing would ever change Okoyong except a consul and a gunboat. She smiled and kept packing.

She left on 4 August 1888 in pouring rain. One young man said to her, with a sob in his voice, “I will constantly pray for you, but you are courting death.” She took five children from her household. It was nearly dark when they landed, with four miles of forest still to walk. As she faced the trees, loud with night noises, fear swept over her. She wanted to turn and run. She tried to pray and couldn't even move her lips. She could only look up and say inside one word: “Father!”

It was enough.

The little procession that walked into Okoyong that night was not impressive: a boy of eleven with a box on his head, a boy of eight crying, a three-year-old crying louder, a girl of five sobbing, and Mary with a baby on her shoulders, pulling herself along by branches and singing nonsense songs to cheer them up.

Ekenge was silent. The chief's mother had died, and everyone had gone to the funeral, which might end in killing. The carriers refused to bring the loads up that night, so Mary went back alone through the dark forest, without boots, fell again and again, woke the paddlers, and had the loads in by midnight. Her feet were so cut that she couldn't wear boots for six weeks. Her first Sunday there, she said, was one of the saddest days she ever spent. She stayed.

Her first victory came at a price. A young slave was accused of sorcery after a woman's death, and the family decided he must die. Mary argued for him while guns and swords were waved in her face, and they agreed to spare his life. But he was still chained, starved, flogged and cut. A life had been saved, and the man had paid for it in his own body. Most of her victories in Okoyong would be like that: real, and only partial.

God told Joshua not to be afraid, which means Joshua was afraid. The reason given wasn't that Joshua was tough. It was “Jehovah thy God is with thee.” Mary walked into Okoyong afraid and stayed there, on and off afraid, for fifteen years. The fear didn't go. She just wasn't alone in it.

When you're too scared to pray properly, one word is a real prayer. Paul says the Spirit teaches us to cry “Abba, Father.” That's the most basic prayer there is.

One thing to do this week: next time you're anxious, a test, a conversation, a dark walk home, try Mary's one-word prayer: “Father.” Then take the next step anyway.

study_questions.question: What was the one prayer Mary could pray at the edge of the forest?
study_questions.answer: Just one word, “Father!” She was too afraid to say anything else, and it was enough.

study_questions.question: Why did Mary go to Okoyong at all?
study_questions.answer: People there were being killed at chiefs' funerals and by the poison ordeal, and no missionary lived there. She went to protect the people most at risk and to bring the gospel.

study_questions.question: Why was her first victory only partial?
study_questions.answer: The accused man's life was spared, but he was still chained, starved, flogged and cut.

fields.title: A Secret Ally
fields.body_html:
“A friend loveth at all times; And a brother is born for adversity.” — Proverbs 17:17 (ASV)

For her first months at Ekenge, Mary lived in one room in the women's yard of Chief Edem's compound, with five children, two cows on the other side of the wall, and goats, rats and cockroaches everywhere. There was no privacy at all. In Okoyong, being left alone was thought terrible, and good manners meant never leaving a guest by herself. Mary longed for silence so she could pray aloud. So she took a machete into the bush and hacked at the undergrowth, praying at the top of her voice so the noise of the blade covered it.

The woman who made those months bearable was the chief's sister, Eme Ete, whom everyone called Ma Eme. She was the widow of a powerful chief. When he died, all his wives had been under suspicion of causing his death, and she had waited for the witch-doctor's verdict. When she was declared innocent, she fainted with the strain. Once Mary noticed marks on her arms and showed her own vaccination scar, thinking they were alike. Ma Eme said simply, “These are the marks of the teeth of my husband.”

She stood between her brother and his wives when he was drunk or angry. And she secretly became Mary's ally. At the risk of her own life, she told Mary who had been accused, who was chained in a farm hut, and when an ordeal or a war was planned. Later they worked out a signal: if Ma Eme learned a killing was coming, she sent a certain bottle to Mary asking for medicine. The chiefs came to believe the white woman could read their minds. A lot of that “second sight” was Ma Eme.

The secret had a cost. When Chief Edem fell ill, people were accused of bewitching him and chained. He recovered, and all were released except one woman, who was put to death. The chief sent word that nobody had been harmed, only a slave woman sold away. Mary knew it was a lie. But if she showed she knew, the chief would hunt for her informant, and scores of people might be made to take the poison to find out who. So she kept quiet. Protecting the person who warned her meant staying silent about a killing. She hated it, and she did it.

The friendship lasted twenty-five years. Ma Eme never became a Christian; she made offerings to the spirits every day of her life. In 1913 the two old women sat together a whole day remembering what they had done “hand in hand in secret.” After Ma Eme died, Mary wrote:

“My dear old friend and almost sister, she made the saving of life so often possible in the early days. It is sad that she did not come out for Christ. She could have been the honoured leader of God's work had she risen to it. I cannot fancy Okoyong without her. She made a foolish choice, and yet God cannot forget all she was to me, and all she helped me to do in those dark and bloody days.”

Mary believed Christ is the only way to God, and she grieved that her friend never came to him. But she would not pretend Ma Eme's mercy wasn't real. Jesus once told a story where the hero was a Samaritan, someone the religious lawyer listening would have looked down on, and asked who had been a neighbour. “He that showed mercy on him,” the lawyer had to answer.

You'll have friends who don't share your faith and who are kinder than some Christians you know. You can hold on to what you believe and still honour their kindness. Leave the judging to God.

One thing to do this week: think of someone outside your faith who has been kind to you. Thank them this week, specifically, for one thing they did.

study_questions.question: How did Ma Eme help Mary save lives?
study_questions.answer: She secretly warned Mary about accusations, ordeals and planned killings, at the risk of her own life, sometimes by sending a signal bottle asking for medicine.

study_questions.question: Why did Mary keep silent when she knew a woman had been killed?
study_questions.answer: If she had shown she knew, the chief would have hunted for her informant and many people might have been put to the poison ordeal.

study_questions.question: How did Mary speak about Ma Eme after her death?
study_questions.answer: She called her “almost sister,” said it was sad she did not come to Christ, and trusted that God could not forget all she had done.

fields.title: “Ifehe!”
fields.body_html:
“Rescue the poor and needy: Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.” — Psalm 82:4 (ASV)

In about 1889 a cheerful Scottish carpenter named Charles Ovens came to Ekenge to build Mary a proper house. He was with her for the hardest fight of her early years.

One morning a strange cry came from the forest. Mary said, “There is something wrong,” and went. Etim, the eldest son of Chief Edem, about to be married, had been struck on the neck by a log and paralysed. She knew what that could mean. “There's going to be trouble,” she told Ovens; “no death of a violent character comes apart from witchcraft.” For two weeks she nursed him. He died. The chief dropped the body into her arms and cried, “Sorcerers have killed and they must die. Bring the witch-doctor.”

The witch-doctor blamed a nearby village. Armed men raided it and brought back more than a dozen men and women in chains.

Mary did something clever. To calm the grieving family, she dressed Etim for burial in silk, in the grand style his rank deserved, and the people were delighted. Then she told Ovens to stop all work. For days and nights they took turns sitting opposite the chained prisoners while men drank and danced around them. Ovens once said he'd get a hammer and chisel and free them himself. “Na, na,” she said. “We'll have a little more patience.”

Then she saw poison beans lying on the pounding stone. She went to her hut and prayed. When she got up, her fear was gone. She told the chiefs there must be no killing, then sat down at the entrance of the yard and would not move. The drunken crowd waved guns and shouted, “Raise our master from the dead, and you shall have the prisoners.”

That night men unchained one woman, a mother, and led her to the body to drink. She was lifting the glass when Mary touched her shoulder and whispered, “Ifehe!” It means “Run.” They ran into the bush together.

The chiefs began releasing prisoners, two, then five, then two more, and stopped. “We have done more for you than we have ever done for any one,” they said, “and we will die before we go further.” Then Ma Eme knelt before her brother and begged him to let Mary keep one of the last women, chained, at her own hut. He agreed. Another woman, Inyam, later crawled to Mary's door in the night, still in chains, having escaped over a roof. Mary guessed someone had helped her, and said nothing. When Etim was buried, the coffin held a cow, not people. For the first time anyone could remember, a man of a chief's family in Okoyong was buried without human sacrifice.

It didn't end cleanly. Fighting followed, and a feud led to a demand of blood for blood. Mary refused to judge that case because she could not bear to sentence a man to death. It went elsewhere, and a young man of twenty, the killer's brother, was put to death in his place. She was in anguish.

Then Edem came to her alone, knelt, and thanked her for forbidding them to take life when his son died. And he said something that changed how she saw everything:

“We are all weary of the old customs, but no single person or House among us has power to break them off, because they are part of the Egbo system.”

Many people in Okoyong wanted out and couldn't break free alone. Mary gave them someone to blame: they could say that Ma would not let them.

Some systems trap everyone in them: bullying in a school, a group chat where everyone joins in because no one dares not to. Sometimes what's needed is one person who sits at the gate and won't move, which lets everyone else stop too.

One thing to do this week: notice one situation this week where people are being treated badly because “that's just how it is.” Be the one who says no, or quietly stands with the person on the receiving end.

study_questions.question: What does “Ifehe!” mean, and when did Mary say it?
study_questions.answer: It means “Run.” She whispered it to a woman who was about to drink the poison, and the two of them ran into the bush.

study_questions.question: What did Chief Edem tell Mary afterwards?
study_questions.answer: That they were all weary of the old customs, but no single person or House could break them because they were part of the Egbo system.

study_questions.question: Why was the victory not complete?
study_questions.answer: Fighting and burning followed, and a young man of twenty was put to death for his brother's crime after Mary refused to judge the case.

She went to her hut and prayed. When she got up, her fear was gone. She told the chiefs there must be no killing, then sat down at the entrance of the yard and would not move. The drunken crowd waved guns and shouted, “Raise our master from the dead, and you shall have the prisoners.” That night men unchained one woman, a mother, and led her to the body to drink. The chiefs began releasing prisoners, two, then five, then two more, and stopped. “We have done more for you than we have ever done for any one,” they said, “and we will die before we go further.” Then Ma Eme knelt before her brother and begged him to let Mary keep one of the last women, chained, at her own hut. Fighting followed, and a feud led to a demand of blood for blood. Mary refused to judge that case because she could not bear to sentence a man to death. It went elsewhere, and a young man of twenty, the killer's brother, was put to death in his place. She was in anguish. Then Edem came to her alone, knelt, and thanked her for forbidding them to take life when his son died. fields.title: “Oh, Susie, Susie!”
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” — Psalm 27:10 (ASV)

Mary's house became a refuge for babies: sick ones left with her to nurse, unwanted ones brought to her, abandoned ones found in the forest.

Many of them died. She dressed each one, laid it in a box among flowers, held a service, and buried it near her house. The little cemetery, her biographer says, “became full of tiny graves.” Ovens tried to comfort her in his own way: “Never mind, lassie, you'll get plenty mair.” The story of Mary and the twins is a rescue story. It is also a story of a woman who kept opening her door knowing that often she would end up digging another grave.

Some lived. One baby girl, whose mother had died, was thrown into the bush beside the market road because of a quarrel between families. She lay there for five days and six nights before women passing by heard a faint cry and mentioned it in Mary's yard. Mary went at once. Ants had injured the baby's face, but she lived, and the same people who had thrown her away came to play with her, calling her “the child of wonder.”

Then came Susie. Her mother, Iye, was a slave woman who was treated well until she gave birth to twins. The English traveller Mary Kingsley happened to be visiting and saw it. Iye's clothes were torn, her treasured basins smashed, and she was driven from the village. The babies were crammed into an empty gin-case on her head. Mary ran barefoot down the forest path, met her, and carried the box herself, because nobody else would touch it. She didn't take Iye down the village path, which would then have been counted as polluted. She stood in the blazing sun while the people cut a new track straight to her house.

The boy had already died from injuries he received when the babies were forced into the box. The girl lived. Iye herself wouldn't hold her, and sang a lament: “Yesterday I was a woman, now I am a horror, a thing all people ran from.”

They named the baby Susie, after Mary's sister. She became the darling of the house. At fourteen months she pulled a jug of boiling water onto herself. For thirteen days and nights Mary hardly put her down. In the dark she'd hear a tiny voice, “Mem, Mem, Mem,” and a little hand held up for a kiss. Early one Sunday Susie died in her arms. “Oh the empty place, and the silence,” Mary wrote. “Oh, Susie, Susie!”

But the village gathered round the grave of a twin, the thing they had once run from, and a leading woman of the old religion stood and praised the white mother's God for the child. Iye, who had grown to love Susie, said, “I have done this. God hates me.” Mary had always refused to buy slaves, but she made one exception. She paid ten pounds for Iye's freedom, and years later Iye was baptised.

A myth needs checking here. Mary Slessor did not end the killing of twins in Nigeria. It had been banned in Calabar before she arrived and went on in some places long after she died. In 1898 she said she had saved fifty-one twins. What she did was carry protection into places the law didn't reach, and wear down fear by living with it. Late in life she came to believe it was better not to take twins away from their mothers at all, but to help families keep them.

The psalm imagines the worst: even your parents abandoning you. For these babies that was real, out of fear more than cruelty. God's answer was a tired woman who went and picked them up.

One thing to do this week: find one way this week to stand with someone others avoid: the new kid, the one people laugh at, the one sitting alone. Sit with them. Carry the box.

fields.title: Laid on His Altar
fields.body_html:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” — Romans 12:1 (ASV)

In 1891 Mary's friends got a surprise: she was engaged. Charles Morrison was a teacher at the mission in Duke Town, a reader and writer, “a man of fine feeling, with a distinct literary gift.” He was twenty-four. She was about forty-two. He had been kind to her when she was ill, and she had few people to talk to about books.

She set one condition from the start. She would not leave Okoyong. He would have to come and work there with her. To a friend she wrote:

“I lay it all in God's hands, and will take from Him whatever He sees best for His work in Okoyong. My life was laid on His altar for that people long ago, and I would not take one jot or tittle of it back.”

The Board said no: his work at Duke Town was too important. Mary said only, “What the Lord ordains is right.” Her biographer adds that she “apparently” put it out of her mind, and that one word is the only hint of what it cost. Morrison's health broke down, he had to leave Calabar, and he later died in America. You may hear that she never married because she was “married to Africa.” The truth is plainer. She wanted to marry. The Church wouldn't send him to Okoyong, she wouldn't leave, and his health failed.

The years that followed were the hardest. In 1896 the people of Okoyong moved inland, and Mary followed to a place called Akpap, living in a two-roomed shed with no floor. A new baby brought an infectious disease into her house, and four of her children died. Then smallpox swept the region. She vaccinated people for hours a day, and turned her old house at Ekenge into a hospital. The sick poured in and everyone else ran.

Edem, the chief who had taken her in eight years before, caught it. She nursed him day and night, and he died in the middle of the night. She was alone. With her own hands she made a coffin, dug a grave and buried him. Then she walked through the dark, wet forest to Akpap and fell onto her bed as dawn broke.

She wrote: “I am just thinking that perhaps the reason God has taken my four bairns is that I may be free to go up and help them.” That's hard to read, and you don't have to agree with it. It was her way of refusing to believe the deaths meant nothing. For a while, her biographer says, she had “no heart for anything.” Today we'd call it grief, and maybe depression. “All is dark,” she wrote in those years, “except above. Calvary stands safe and sure.”

Then for three years she worked alone, often ill and unable to sleep. When she wrote up her first seven years in Okoyong, she had to report no baptisms at all. “Christ sent me to preach the Gospel,” she said, “and He will look after results.”

Paul says to offer your whole self to God as a “living sacrifice.” Mary did, and it cost her a marriage, four children and a friend she buried herself. She didn't think God had cheated her. But she never pretended it was easy, and you don't have to either.

If you've felt “no heart for anything” for weeks, that's not a spiritual failure. Tell a safe person: a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor, or a crisis line where you live. Mary kept going partly because others were praying and writing to her. You need people too.

One thing to do this week: think of one thing you're holding back from God, a plan, a relationship, a dream. Write it down and pray, honestly, “I lay it in your hands.” If you've been low for a long time, tell one trusted person this week.

fields.title: The Woman's God
fields.body_html:
“He hath showed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth Jehovah require of thee, but to do justly, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with thy God?” — Micah 6:8 (ASV)

Early in her Okoyong years a message came from a chief eight hours' walk away. He was dying, and his people stood outside his house armed, because when a chief died his household might be killed. Everyone told Mary she couldn't go. She went, through rain so heavy that she lost her boots, her stockings, her umbrella and most of her clothes, which the women escorting her carried in calabashes. She later learned that nothing ever won the hearts of Okoyong like that walk. The chief recovered. No one died.

Later, word came of a war about to start at dawn. She was ill and was told the forest would be full of armed men firing at anything. She asked a chief for a man to beat the Egbo drum before her. He sent back a polite non-answer, adding that a woman who went into a war only proved her ignorance. She sent back a reply that's still remembered:

“In measuring the woman's power, you have evidently forgotten to take into account the woman's God.”

At the enemy village a silent wall of armed men stood waiting. An old man stepped out and knelt at her feet, asking her to help make peace. It was the chief she had walked through the rain to heal.

At palavers she knitted. It kept her from showing fear, and the needles clicking calmly in the middle of the shouting calmed everyone down.

Then British power arrived. In the 1890s Britain declared a protectorate over the region, and where treaties were refused it sent gunboats and soldiers. People in Okoyong came to link the consul with “big guns and burnt towns.” The British commissioner, Sir Claude Macdonald, respected Mary, and asked her to run a native court in Okoyong. She did it unpaid.

A British official watched her court. He found “a little frail old lady” rocking a baby. Suddenly she jumped up, grabbed a rude chief by the neck, boxed his ears and threw him out, then sat down again. In one case a man won a debt, and Mary ordered him caned in front of everyone anyway, for neglecting his mother and children and much else. The official loved it. But be honest about it: he was beaten for things he hadn't been charged with, with no appeal. Her justice depended entirely on her being right. Often she was. Not always.

She also lived with a hard tension. Some chiefs, after a funeral passed without killing, told her, “Ma, you white people are God Almighty. No other power could have done this.” They weren't wrong about where power lay: behind her stood the consul, and behind him, guns. In 1901 a British army invaded the Aro country to the west. In the middle of that, Mary wrote something rare for a European then: “After all we are foreigners, and they own the country, so I always try to make the law fit in, while we adjust things between us.”

Later, at Itu, she sat as a magistrate, refusing any salary, mainly to protect women. “God help these poor helpless women!” she wrote after a day of cases of chained, branded and beaten wives. Husbands who had deserted their wives for bearing twins were summoned, and every one agreed to take his wife back. (She's often called the first woman magistrate in the British Empire, but that's never been proved.)

Micah says God wants three things: justice, kindness and humility. Mary had plenty of the first two. Humility towards the people she governed grew more slowly. Power, even used for good, is dangerous, and she didn't always handle it well.

You'll have power over someone: a younger sibling, a team, a group chat. Use it to protect people, and remember you can be wrong.

One thing to do this week: next time you're in charge of anything, ask Micah's three questions: Is this fair? Is this kind? Am I being humble? Change one thing if the answer is no.

study_questions.question: What did Mary mean by “the woman's God”?
study_questions.answer: The chief judged her by her own weakness as a woman. She was saying that her power came from God, not from herself.

fields.title: “I Dare Not Go Back”
fields.body_html:
“But Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” — Luke 9:62 (ASV)

In August 1903, fifteen years after she walked into Okoyong, the first communion service in the district was held at Akpap. Seven young Christians were baptised, and Mary presented eleven children for baptism, six of them children she had rescued. The people sang Psalm 103 in Efik: “Who redeemeth thy life from destruction.” She had watched lives taken there for fifteen years. Now Okoyong people were singing about a God who rescues life. She told the newly baptised, “Okoyong now looks to you more than to me for proof of the power of the Gospel.”

One of the first Christians was Akom, a woman who had once helped send a chief's wives and slaves to their deaths. When a man who had falsely accused her of witchcraft came to make friends, she said, “I sometimes wanted to take revenge, but I have got it from God, and His revenge is of a sweeter kind than that of the Consul.”

That year Mary also did something new. Itu, on the Cross River, had been a slave market for centuries. She took three young people there and left them: two boys, Esien and Effiom, and Mana, a girl who had been kidnapped as a child and sold as a slave. Esien was to lead services, Effiom the singing, and Mana to teach the girls. Within months the congregation numbered more than three hundred, in a church the people built themselves. Her biographer says plainly who was behind it: Mana, “a black slave-girl,” who had taught and nursed the women of Itu “as a mother might.” The church at Itu owed its first life not to a Scottish missionary but to an African girl who had once been bought and sold.

Up the Enyong Creek lived a chief named Onoyom. Grieving a dead child and hunting the man he believed had bewitched him, he met a former mission teacher who had fallen into drink and was homeless. “Where can I find this God?” Onoyom asked. “I am not worthy to say,” the man answered, “but go to the white Ma at Itu, and she will tell you.” Onoyom later built a church with his own savings, and chose for its seats a great tree his town treated as a shrine. “God is stronger than juju,” he said.

Mary built too. She laid cement floors herself. “I just stir it like porridge, turn it out, smooth it with a stick, and all the time keep praying, 'Lord, here's the cement, if to Thy glory, set it,' and it has never once gone wrong.”

Mary first reached Arochukwu, the Aro heartland, in 1903 under the escort of the colonel whose army had conquered it, and partly to get there before Roman Catholic missionaries. Historians who see her as a servant of empire have fair evidence on their side.

By 1906 the mission's rules said she had to return to Okoyong. She was nearly sixty, ill, and could no longer walk far. But she had people begging, “Give us even a boy!” “There is an impelling power behind me, and I dare not look backward,” she said. “Even if it cost me my connection with the Church of my heart's love, I feel I must go forward.” In the end the Church gave way and freed her to work as a pioneer.

The verse at the top is one of Jesus' hardest sayings. A ploughman who keeps looking over his shoulder cuts a crooked line. Mary loved Okoyong and was afraid of losing her Church, and it made her “mutinous” and hard to manage. It also opened the Creek to the gospel.

Notice too how the gospel actually travelled: a homeless drunk, a former slave girl, two teenage boys. God uses the people nobody puts on a poster.

One thing to do this week: do one thing this week you've been putting off because it's new and uncomfortable: a conversation, a club, an apology. Put your hand to the plough and don't look back.

study_questions.question: Who started the church at Itu?
study_questions.answer: Mana, a former slave girl, with two boys, Esien and Effiom. Mana taught and nursed the women “as a mother might.”

study_questions.question: How did Onoyom first hear about Mary?
study_questions.answer: A homeless former mission teacher who had fallen into drink told him, “go to the white Ma at Itu, and she will tell you.”

study_questions.question: Why did Mary say “I dare not go back”?
study_questions.answer: She felt God pushing her forward into new places on the Creek, and could not abandon them to return to Okoyong, even if it cost her connection with her Church.

She told the newly baptised, “Okoyong now looks to you more than to me for proof of the power of the Gospel.” One of the first Christians was Akom, a woman who had once helped send a chief's wives and slaves to their deaths. When a man who had falsely accused her of witchcraft came to make friends, she said, “I sometimes wanted to take revenge, but I have got it from God, and His revenge is of a sweeter kind than that of the Consul.” That year Mary also did something new. Itu, on the Cross River, had been a slave market for centuries. She took three young people there and left them: two boys, Esien and Effiom, and Mana, a girl who had been kidnapped as a child and sold as a slave. Esien was to lead services, Effiom the singing, and Mana to teach the girls. Within months the congregation numbered more than three hundred, in a church the people built themselves. Her biographer says plainly who was behind it: Mana, “a black slave-girl,” who had taught and nursed the women of Itu “as a mother might.” The church at Itu owed its first life not to a Scottish missionary but to an African girl who had once been bought and sold. Up the Enyong Creek lived a chief named Onoyom. Grieving a dead child and hunting the man he believed had bewitched him, he met a former mission teacher who had fallen into drink and was homeless. “Where can I find this God?” Onoyom asked. “I am not worthy to say,” the man answered, “but go to the white Ma at Itu, and she will tell you.” Onoyom later built a church with his own savings, and chose for its seats a great tree his town treated as a shrine. “God is stronger than juju,” he said. Mary built too. She laid cement floors herself. “I just stir it like porridge, turn it out, smooth it with a stick, and all the time keep praying, 'Lord, here's the cement, if to Thy glory, set it,' and it has never once gone wrong.” Mary first reached Arochukwu, the Aro heartland, in 1903 under the escort of the colonel whose army had conquered it, and partly to get there before Roman Catholic missionaries. Historians who see her as a servant of empire have fair evidence on their side. By 1906 the mission's rules said she had to return to Okoyong. She was nearly sixty, ill, and could no longer walk far. But she had people begging, “Give us even a boy!” “There is an impelling power behind me, and I dare not look backward,” she said. “Even if it cost me my connection with the Church of my heart's love, I feel I must go forward.” In the end the Church gave way and freed her to work as a pioneer. The verse at the top is one of Jesus' hardest sayings. A ploughman who keeps looking over his shoulder cuts a crooked line. Mary loved Okoyong and was afraid of losing her Church, and it made her “mutinous” and hard to manage. It also opened the Creek to the gospel. Notice too how the gospel actually travelled: a homeless drunk, a former slave girl, two teenage boys. God uses the people nobody puts on a poster. One thing to do this week: do one thing this week you've been putting off because it's new and uncomfortable: a conversation, a club, an apology. Put your hand to the plough and don't look back.

fields.title: Safe
fields.body_html:
“And he hath said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (ASV)

Past sixty, Mary was carried to church. Young men at Ikpe, an old slave-trading town two days up the Creek, were building a church with no one to teach them. She begged her Church to send two women. None came. “I must go,” she said. “I am in honour bound to go.” She lived in two rooms behind the church with a camp-bed. For the canoe journeys she took laudanum, the painkiller of the time, and lay wrapped in a blanket in the bottom of the boat.

“I'm a wee, wee wifie, verra little buikit, but I grip on well, none the less,” she wrote. “I begin every day,” she said, “almost every journey in pain, and in such tiredness that I am sure I can't go on, and whenever I begin, the strength comes, and it increases.”

She still lost. At Ikpe twins were born. By now she believed it was better not to take twins from their mother, so the baby boy stayed with her, and Mary's daughter Jean slept beside them for ten weeks. One Sunday the mother hurt the baby and gave him poison. He recovered, and the parents took him home. Four days later Jean carried him back, dying. After nearly forty years, Mary could still lose. Beliefs change slowly.

She didn't pretend her faith was strong. “I am a poor exponent of faith,” she said. “I ought to have full faith in our Father that He will do everything, but I am ashamed of myself, for I want to 'see,' and that sends faith out of court. I never felt more in sympathy with that old afflicted father before in his prayer, 'Lord, I believe, help Thou my unbelief.' Every syllable suits me.” In 1913 she was given a royal honour and hid from the fuss, signing herself “the unworthy, unprofitable, but most willing, servant of the King of Kings.”

In 1914 war broke out in Europe, and she fell seriously ill. Her church boys carried her in her camp-bed and paddled her down the Creek. On 5 January 1915 she wrote to a mother whose sons had gone to war: “In God's governance not one precious thing can ever be lost.” A few days later the fever came back. Once she prayed in Efik, “O Abasi, sana mi yok”: “O God, release me.”

At half past three in the morning on 13 January 1915, at Use, Mary Slessor died, aged sixty-six. The girls she had raised were around her. When they understood, they cried out in grief and fear: “We shall be counted as slaves now that our mother is dead.” She had given them love, a home and a name, but she couldn't give them a safe place in a society where a child without a family had no protection. They knew it.

People came from the whole district to mourn Eka kpukpru owo, “Everybody's Mother.” She was buried on the hill above Duke Town, where she had first landed thirty-nine years before. At the graveside sat Mammy Fuller, the Jamaican nurse who had been her friend since her first months in Calabar. When women began to wail, the old woman stood up. “Do not cry, do not cry. Praise God from whom all blessings flow. Ma was a great blessing.” As the coffin went down, she said one word: “Safe.”

Paul asked God to take away his weakness, and God said no: “My grace is sufficient for thee.” Mary was never made strong. She was given enough strength to begin, each morning. Her faith was often weak by her own account, her temper sharp, her views sometimes the views of her time. But no one who knew her doubted her love.

You don't have to feel strong to start. Start, and see whether the strength comes.

One thing to do this week: pick the thing you feel too tired or too weak to begin. Pray Paul's verse, “My grace is sufficient for thee,” and then just begin, for ten minutes. Notice what happens.

study_questions.question: How did Mary describe the strength she was given in old age?
study_questions.answer: She began every day in pain and tiredness, sure she couldn't go on, “and whenever I begin, the strength comes, and it increases.”

study_questions.question: Why did the girls cry “We shall be counted as slaves”?
study_questions.answer: Without Mary, they had no family to protect them in a society where a child without family had no standing.

study_questions.question: What did Mammy Fuller say at the grave?
study_questions.answer: She told the mourners not to cry, said “Ma was a great blessing,” and as the coffin went down said one word: “Safe.”
